## Fit all
for(i in seq_along(res)) {
    for(j in seq_along(res[[i]])) {
        t1 <- make_datetime(year = min(seq[[i]][[j]]))
        t2 <- make_datetime(year = max(seq[[i]][[j]]), month = 12, day = 31, hour = 23, min = 50)
        n1 <- names(seq)[[i]]
        n2 <- names(seq[[i]])[[j]]
        fl <- here::here("rds", sprintf("fit-%s-%s-%s.rds", n1, n2, st_id))
        if(!file.exists(fl)) {
            res[[i]][[j]] <- with(subset(db_comp, time >= t1 & time <= t2), fit_th(x = sea_level, dto = time, pred = FALSE))
            saveRDS(res[[i]][[j]], fl)
        } else {
            res[[i]][[j]] <- readRDS(fl)
        }
    }
}







K1, O1, M2, and S2 are the main tidal constituents because they represent the dominant astronomical forcing mechanisms and typically have the largest amplitudes.

Semi-diurnal constituents (2 cycles per day):

M2 (Principal lunar semi-diurnal): The largest tidal constituent in most places. Period = 12.42 hours. Caused by the moon’s gravitational pull as Earth rotates beneath it.
S2 (Principal solar semi-diurnal): Second largest semi-diurnal constituent. Period = 12.00 hours. Caused by the sun’s gravitational pull.

Diurnal constituents (1 cycle per day):

K1 (Lunisolar diurnal): Largest diurnal constituent. Period = 23.93 hours. Results from the declination of the moon and sun.
O1 (Principal lunar diurnal): Second largest diurnal constituent. Period = 25.82 hours. Due to lunar declination effects.


Why these four matters:

Largest amplitudes: They typically account for 70-90% of tidal variance
Physical significance:

M2 & S2 create spring-neap cycles (14-day variation)
K1 & O1 create diurnal inequality (different heights of successive high/low tides)

Tidal classification: The form factor (K1+O1)/(M2+S2) uses these to classify whether tides are semi-diurnal, diurnal, or mixed
Coastal features: MHWS, MLWS, etc. are primarily defined by M2 and S2

The following figure shows how the estimated amplitudes of the four tidal constituents — K1, M2, O1 and S2 — vary through time at Galway Port. Results are shown separately for the rolling 3-year (y_3) and 5-year (y_5) fitting windows. The red dashed line provides a reference value for each constituent, allowing changes in the rolling estimates to be viewed relative to the longer-term estimate.
The clearest temporal changes occur for the two semidiurnal constituents, M2 and S2. M2 has the largest amplitude, confirming that it is the dominant constituent among those shown. Its estimated amplitude is relatively high in the earlier windows before declining noticeably from around 2012–2015. It subsequently stabilises at a lower level. S2 exhibits a very similar pattern, falling from approximately 0.566 m in the earliest windows to around 0.550–0.552 m in the later part of the record. The similarity between the 3- and 5-year results suggests that these patterns are not simply an artefact of the particular window length used.
K1 shows a smaller but still systematic change through time. Its amplitude initially increases slightly, before declining in the later windows. By approximately 2018 onwards, both the 3- and 5-year estimates lie below the reference value.
In contrast, O1 is relatively stable. Its amplitude is much smaller, and although the 3-year estimates fluctuate somewhat, there is no change comparable in magnitude to that seen for M2 and S2. The smoother 5-year estimates remain close to the longer-term reference for much of the record.
As expected, the 3-year windows show greater short-term variability, whereas the 5-year windows produce smoother trajectories because each estimate incorporates a longer period of observations. Importantly, however, the main temporal patterns are broadly consistent between the two window lengths.
These temporal changes in the estimated tidal constituents may be expected to subsequently feed into the estimates of derived tidal characteristics such as MHWS, MHWN, MLWN and MLWS, which motivates modelling the tidal features through time rather than relying only on a single estimate calculated from the entire record.


Show code
## Extract constituent amplitudes
constituent_amps <- map(res, \(x) map(x, \(y) {
  coefs <- y$coefficients
  tibble(
    K1 = sqrt(coefs["K1_C"]^2 + coefs["K1_S"]^2),
    O1 = sqrt(coefs["O1_C"]^2 + coefs["O1_S"]^2),
    M2 = sqrt(coefs["M2_C"]^2 + coefs["M2_S"]^2),
    S2 = sqrt(coefs["S2_C"]^2 + coefs["S2_S"]^2)
  )
})) |>
  imap_dfr(function(window_list, window_name) {
    imap_dfr(window_list, function(amps, year_range) {
      amps |>
        mutate(window_size = window_name, year_range = year_range, .before = 1)
    })
  }) |>
  mutate(
    n_years = as.integer(str_extract(window_size, "\\d+")),
    year_end = as.integer(str_extract(year_range, "(?<=y)\\d+")),
    year_start = as.integer(str_extract(year_range, "\\d+$")),
    year_mid = (year_start + year_end) / 2) |>
  pivot_longer(cols = c(K1, O1, M2, S2), names_to = "constituent", values_to = "amplitude")

## Plot
## Extract the last values for plotting
ly <- constituent_amps$window_size |> tail(1)
amps_ref <- constituent_amps |>
    filter(window_size == ly) |>
    select(constituent, amplitude)
## Plot with horizontal reference lines
constituent_amps |>
    filter(window_size != ly) |>
    ggplot(aes(x = make_datetime(year_mid), y = amplitude)) +
    geom_hline(data = amps_ref, aes(yintercept = amplitude), linetype = "dashed", color = "red", alpha = 0.7) +
    geom_line() +
    geom_point() +
    facet_grid(constituent ~ window_size, scales = "free_y") +
    scale_x_datetime(date_breaks = "2 year", date_minor_breaks = "1 year", date_labels = "%Y") +
    labs(x = "Midpoint Year", y = "Amplitude (m)", title = "Tidal Constituent Amplitudes Over Time")












The form factor is calculated by
\[(K1+O1)/(M2+S2)\]
and it classifies tides as:

< 0.25: Semi-diurnal
0.25-1.5: Mixed, mainly semi-diurnal
1.5-3.0: Mixed, mainly diurnal
> 3.0: Diurnal

The following figure shows how the tidal form factor at Galway Port varies through time, estimated using the rolling 3-year and 5-year fitting windows. The red dashed line represents the form factor estimated from the longer-term record and provides a reference against which the rolling estimates can be compared.
The form factor remains within a very narrow range, approximately 0.083–0.086, throughout the record. Both window lengths show a similar pattern: values are relatively low in the earlier windows, increase to a maximum around 2014–2017, and decline again towards the later years.
The 3-year estimates show somewhat greater year-to-year variability, as expected because they are calculated from shorter periods of data. The 5-year estimates are smoother, but reproduce the same general rise and subsequent decline. This agreement indicates that the pattern is not simply a consequence of the choice of rolling-window length.
Most importantly, the form factor remains well below 0.25 throughout the entire record. This indicates that Galway Port has a semidiurnal tidal regime.

Tidal levels (or features) are defined as:

HAT (Highest Astronomical Tide) = maximum predicted astronomical tide over the reference prediction period
MSL (Mean Sea Level) = mean of the time series (or the constant/mean term in the model)
MHWS (Mean High Water Springs) = MSL + M2\(_{\text{amp}}\) + S2\(_{\text{amp}}\)
MHWN (Mean High Water Neaps) = MSL + M2\(_{\text{amp}}\) - S2\(_{\text{amp}}\)
MLWN (Mean Low Water Neaps) = MSL - M2\(_{\text{amp}}\) + S2\(_{\text{amp}}\)
MLWS (Mean Low Water Springs) = MSL - M2\(_{\text{amp}}\) - S2\(_{\text{amp}}\)
LAT (Lowest Astronomical Tide) = minimum predicted astronomical tide over the reference prediction period

Where:

M2 = principal lunar semi-diurnal (largest constituent)
S2 = principal solar semi-diurnal

Springs occur when M2 and S2 are in phase (add together), creating the highest highs and lowest lows.
Neaps occur when M2 and S2 are out of phase (subtract), creating smaller tidal ranges.
The following figure shows the estimated tidal levels at Galway Port through time, derived from the harmonic models fitted using rolling 3-year and 5-year windows. The tidal characteristics shown are HAT, MHWS, MHWN, MSL, MLWN, MLWS and LAT. The red dashed lines provide the corresponding longer-term estimates for comparison.
In earlier windows, the high-water levels (particularly HAT and MHWS) tend to be higher, while the low-water levels (particularly MLWS and LAT) tend to be lower. Moving into the middle and later parts of the record, the high-water estimates generally decrease and the low-water estimates become less negative. This indicates a narrowing of the estimated tidal range relative to the earlier part of the record.
This pattern is particularly evident for HAT and LAT. HAT declines from around 3.0 m in the earlier windows to around 2.9 m in the later windows, while LAT moves from values below approximately −3.0 m towards values closer to −2.9 m. Similar, though smaller, changes are visible for MHWS and MLWS. These patterns are consistent with the earlier constituent analysis, where the amplitudes of the dominant semidiurnal constituents M2 and S2 decreased between the earlier and later fitting windows.
The intermediate tidal levels, MHWN and MLWN, also vary through time but over a narrower range. MHWN generally decreases during the first half of the record before showing some recovery in the most recent windows, while MLWN becomes less negative overall.
In contrast, MSL remains comparatively stable, fluctuating only by a few centimetres around approximately 0.04–0.05 m OD Malin.

title: Exploring the Tide-Gauge Data
text:
Duplicate Stations
The tide gauge station at Malin Head appears in both sources. However, when the temporal structure of each dataset is examined, it reveals no overlap in recordings. The Marine Institute tide gauge collected data from 2004 to 2008, and the OPW tide gauge began recordings approximately eight months later. Because there is no overlap here, both will be kept for analysis.


Show code
station_source_overlap <- da |>
  distinct(st_id, source) |>
  count(st_id, name = "n_sources") |>
  filter(n_sources > 1)


## Investigate duplicate sources for MalinHead-PortmorePier
da |>

section: Geographic Distribution of Tide Gauge Stations
text:
Geographic Distribution of Tide Gauge Stations
The following plot presents the geographic distribution of Irish tide gauge stations, coloured according to their source (MI or OPW).


Show code
ireland <- rnaturalearth::ne_countries(scale = "medium", country = "Ireland", returnclass = "sf")

station_locations <- da |>
  filter(!is.na(latitude), !is.na(longitude)) |>
  group_by(source, st_id, station_id) |>
  summarise(latitude = first(latitude), longitude = first(longitude), .groups = "drop") |>
  sf::st_as_sf(coords = c("longitude", "latitude"), crs = 4326)

ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data = ireland, fill = "grey95", colour = "grey40") +
  geom_sf(data = station_locations, aes(colour = source), size = 2.5) +
  coord_sf(xlim = c(-11, -5.5), ylim = c(51.2, 55.6), expand = FALSE) +
  labs(x = "Longitude", y = "Latitude", colour = "Source") +
  theme_bw()+
  theme(panel.background = element_rect(fill = "aliceblue", colour = NA))

title: Exploring the Tide-Gauge Data
text:
Temporal coverage
The duration of a tide-gauge record alone does not describe how much information is available. The first analysis therefore examines the beginning, end and total span of the record at each station.


Show code
MIN_RECORD_YEARS <- 3

station_coverage <- da |>
  group_by(source, st_id, station_id) |>
  summarise(first_obs = min(time, na.rm = TRUE), last_obs = max(time, na.rm = TRUE), n_observations = n(),.groups = "drop") |>
  mutate(
    record_days = as.numeric(difftime(last_obs, first_obs, units = "days")),
    record_years = record_days / 365.25,
    include_analysis = record_years >= MIN_RECORD_YEARS,
    exclusion_reason = if_else(include_analysis, NA_character_, "Less than 3 years of available data")) |>
  arrange(record_years)


station_coverage |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 2, format = "html", format.args = list(big.mark = ",")) |>
  kableExtra::kable_styling(full_width = TRUE, bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover", "condensed")) |>
  kableExtra::scroll_box(height = "500px", fixed_thead = TRUE)

Galway Port 2, Tivoli Docks and Bantry have fewer than three years of observations each. As a result, they will be removed from the analysis.


Show code
station_coverage |>
  mutate(station_id = fct_reorder(station_id, first_obs)) |>
  ggplot(aes(y = station_id)) +
  geom_segment( aes(x = first_obs, xend = last_obs, yend = station_id, colour = source), linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(aes(x = first_obs, colour=source), size = 1.8) +
  geom_point(aes(x = last_obs, colour=source), size = 1.8) +
  scale_x_datetime(date_breaks = "5 years", date_labels = "%Y") +
  labs(title = "Temporal Coverage of Tide-Gauge Stations", x = "Year", y = NULL, colour = "Source") +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(size = 16, face = "bold"),
    axis.title.x = element_text(size = 12),
    axis.text.x = element_text(size = 9),
    axis.text.y = element_text(size = 9),
    panel.grid.major.y = element_line(linewidth = 0.3),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    legend.position = "right")









The plot shows variation in the temporal coverage of the tide-gauge records, both between stations and between the MI and OPW data sources. Record lengths range from only a few years for some stations to more than two decades for the longest-running gauges.
The MI stations generally provide the longer historical records. Several stations, including Galway Port, Killybegs Port, Inishmore and Castletownbere Port, have records extending back to approximately 2007, while Malin Head–Portmore Pier extends even further back. Some MI records are considerably shorter, however, particularly stations such as Galway Port 2 and Howth Water Level 2, which only cover relatively recent years. Skerries Harbour and Dublin Port are notable because their records end substantially earlier than most of the other MI stations.
The OPW contribution is particularly important for extending the geographical network with more recent observations. Many OPW stations begin around 2019–2021 and continue to the end of the study period. A smaller number have much longer records: Adelphi Quay extends back to around 2000, while Port Oriel, Rossaveel Pier and Fenit provide records extending back to approximately 2007–2011.


Show code
observations_year <- da |>
  mutate(year = year(time)) |>
  count(source, st_id, station_id, year, name = "n")

observations_year |>
  ggplot(aes(x = year, y = n)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.7) +
  geom_point(size = 1.2) +
  facet_wrap(~ station_id, scales = "free_y", ncol = 4) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = scales::pretty_breaks(n = 4)) +
  scale_y_continuous(
    labels = scales::label_number(scale_cut = scales::cut_short_scale()),
    breaks = scales::pretty_breaks(n = 4)) +
  labs(title = "Number of Observations per Year", x = "Year", y = "Number of observations") +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(size = 16, face = "bold"),
    axis.title = element_text(size = 12),
    axis.text = element_text(size = 9),
    axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1),
    strip.text = element_text(size = 9),
    panel.spacing = unit(0.8, "lines"))









This plot provides a more detailed view of how the amount of available data varies through time within each station record. While the temporal-coverage plot shows when each station begins and ends, this figure shows that having a station record spanning a particular period does not necessarily mean that observations are equally complete throughout that period.
For many stations, the annual number of observations is relatively stable during the main part of the record. Several stations have approximately 90,000–105,000 observations per year, suggesting a high and reasonably consistent sampling frequency. Other stations have lower but similarly stable annual counts, which likely reflects differences in their underlying sampling frequency rather than necessarily poorer data quality.
There are, however, clear examples of substantial variation in data availability within individual records. Malin Head–Portmore Pier is particularly variable, with pronounced reductions in the number of observations in several years. Port Oriel, Skerries Harbour, Sligo, Inishmore and Ballyglass Harbour also show sizeable year-to-year changes. These reductions indicate periods of missing observations, changes in sampling frequency, or both, and warrant further investigation before modelling.
The very low counts occurring at the beginning or end of many station records should be interpreted differently. For example, a number of stations fall close to zero in their final year. These values do not necessarily represent poor-quality years; they can arise because the dataset contains only a partial calendar year at the start or end of the available record. This is particularly important for the most recent year in the dataset. Annual observation counts therefore need to be interpreted alongside the dates of the first and last observations.

title: Exploring the Tide-Gauge Data
text:
Sampling frequency
The plot above suggests that stations are not all recording observations at the same temporal resolution. Sampling frequency may also change through time at individual stations. The following calculations use the difference between consecutive observed timestamps to determine the most likely sampling frequency for each station.


Show code
sampling_intervals <- da |>
  select(source, st_id, station_id, time) |>
  arrange(st_id, time) |>
  group_by(st_id) |>
  mutate(dtime = as.numeric(difftime( time, lag(time), units = "mins"))) |>
  ungroup() |>
  filter(!is.na(dtime), dtime > 0)


The table below contains the expected sampling interval for each station, along with the number of times that sampling interval was detected during the tide gauge record. The majority of stations (both MI and OPW) have an expected sampling interval of every five or six minutes, with a handful of stations that appear to have the slightly longer 15-minute sampling interval.


Show code
station_sampling_frequency <- sampling_intervals |>
  count(source, st_id, station_id, dtime, name = "n_interval") |>
  group_by(source, st_id, station_id) |>
  slice_max(n_interval, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE) |>
  ungroup() |>
  rename(expected_interval_min = dtime) |>
  arrange(source, expected_interval_min, station_id)

  knitr::kable(digits = 2)

This plot shows the median time interval between consecutive water-level observations for each station and year.
Most stations have a high and very consistent sampling frequency. A large proportion of the more recent records have a median sampling interval of approximately 5 minutes, while several of the longer-running MI stations initially recorded observations at approximately 6-minute intervals. Stations including Galway Port, Inishmore, Ballycotton Harbour, Ballyglass Harbour and Dunmore East Harbour show a clear transition from approximately 6-minute to 5-minute sampling in the later part of their records. These systematic shifts are likely to reflect changes in the data collection or recording regime rather than changes in data quality.
The figure identifies two conspicuous anomalies: Kilrush Lough and Roonagh Pier have extremely large median intervals in the final part of their records. These values are several orders of magnitude larger than those observed elsewhere and are unlikely to represent genuine sampling frequencies. Instead, they suggest that very few observations remain during those years, producing very large time gaps between consecutive measurements. These stations should therefore be examined when assessing missingness and deciding which years are sufficiently complete for analysis.
Malin Head–Portmore Pier also differs from most stations, showing some variation between approximately 5- and 6-minute intervals during the earlier portion of its record before settling at approximately 5 minutes. This could reflect changes in recording frequency or interruptions within the historical record.

title: Exploring the Tide-Gauge Data
text:
Missing data and gaps
A long record can still contain substantial periods with no observations. Consequently, both the duration and completeness of each record are examined.
A gap is defined relative to the station’s usual sampling interval. For example, if a station normally records every 10 minutes, an interval greater than 10 minutes indicates that at least one expected observation is absent.
The issue identified with Roonagh Pier in the above plot is explained here by the large gap in the record for this station. Roonagh Pier has an expected sampling interval of every six minutes, but has a gap in the sampling of approximately 2,486 days (or approximately 6.8 years).
Roonagh Pier is not the only tide gauge station with a large gap in its record. Stations such as Inishmore, Sligo, and Wexford Harbour also have large amounts of missing data. The difference, as we will see in subsequent plots, is that for the Roonagh Pier station, a large gap in the data is combined with a relatively short sampling time, whereas the other stations have longer sampling records.


Show code
gap_data <- sampling_intervals |>
  left_join(
    station_sampling_frequency |>
      select(source, st_id, station_id, expected_interval_min),
    by = c("source", "st_id", "station_id")) |>
  mutate(
    is_gap = dtime > expected_interval_min,
    missing_intervals = pmax(round(dtime / expected_interval_min) - 1, 0))

gap_data |>
  filter(is_gap) |>
  select(source, station_id, st_id, time, dtime, expected_interval_min, missing_intervals) |>
  arrange(desc(dtime)) |>
  slice_head(n = 30) |>
  mutate(gap_hours = dtime / 60, gap_days = dtime / (60 * 24)) |>
  select(source, station_id, time, expected_interval_min, gap_hours, gap_days, missing_intervals) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 2, format = "html", format.args = list(big.mark = ",")) |>
  kableExtra::kable_styling(full_width = TRUE, bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover", "condensed")) |>
  kableExtra::scroll_box(height = "500px", fixed_thead = TRUE)

This heatmap provides an assessment of data completeness within each station record, showing the percentage of expected observations that are available in each calendar year. Dark purple represents years approaching 100% completeness, while lighter blue, green and yellow indicate progressively less complete years. White areas correspond to periods outside the available station record and/or periods of missing data.
A strong feature of the plot is that many stations have very high completeness during the main portion of their records. For example, Adelphi Quay, Dublin Port, Fenit, Galway Port, Killybegs Port and Ringsaskiddy NMCI contain long sequences of predominantly dark-purple cells. This indicates that, once these stations were operational, most expected observations were available for many consecutive years.
There are also examples of discontinuous records. Inishmore and Skerries Harbour contain substantial gaps between periods of available data, while Roonagh Pier has a break within its relatively short record. These gaps are important because a station’s first and last observation alone would make the record appear substantially more complete than it actually is.
Roonagh Pier, in particular is notable here. While previous checks did not flag Roonagh Pier as having fewer than three years of data, this heatmap shows us that it has two consecutive years of data, followed by a long gap, and then its final year of data is collected in 2024. This suggests that Roonagh Pier will not be a suitable station for further analysis.
While Inishmore has a similarly large gap in the data record, the fact that it has a much longer record overall means it is suitable for analysis, though the gap between approximately 2010 and 2016 will need to be taken into account at the modelling stage.
Another prominent feature is the low completeness in 2024 for many stations, visible as the yellow or green column at the right-hand side of the heatmap. Because this occurs simultaneously across a large number of otherwise highly complete stations, it is much more likely to reflect a partial final year in the dataset than a widespread deterioration in station performance. The final calendar year should therefore not be interpreted in the same way as an incomplete year occurring in the middle of a station’s record.


Show code
annual_completeness <- da |>
  mutate(year = year(time)) |>
  group_by(source, st_id, station_id, year) |>
  summarise(
    first_obs_year = min(time, na.rm = TRUE),
    last_obs_year = max(time, na.rm = TRUE),
    n_observed = n(), .groups = "drop") |>
  left_join(
    station_sampling_frequency |>
      select(source, st_id, station_id, expected_interval_min),
    by = c("source", "st_id", "station_id")) |>
  mutate(
    active_minutes = as.numeric(difftime(last_obs_year, first_obs_year, units = "mins")),
    n_expected = floor(active_minutes / expected_interval_min) + 1,
    completeness =pmin(n_observed / n_expected, 1),
    completeness_percent = 100 * completeness)

annual_completeness |>
  mutate(station_id = fct_rev(factor(station_id))) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = year, y = station_id, fill = completeness_percent)) +
  geom_tile(colour = "white", linewidth = 0.1) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(limits = c(0, 100),  direction = -1, name = "Complete (%)") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = scales::pretty_breaks(n = 8)) +
  labs(title = "Annual Completeness of Tide-Gauge Records", x = "Year",  y = NULL) +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(size = 16, face = "bold"),
    axis.title.x = element_text(size = 12),
    axis.text.x = element_text(size = 9),
    axis.text.y = element_text(size = 9),
    panel.grid = element_blank(),
    legend.position = "right")

title: Exploring the Tide-Gauge Data
text:
Water-level observations
This plot compares the distribution of observed water levels across stations, with stations ordered by their median water level. The boxes represent the interquartile range, the central lines show the median, and the whiskers describe the spread of the observations beyond the central 50% of the data.
For the majority of stations, the distributions are broadly comparable. Median water levels are generally close to 0 m OD Malin, while most stations show similar variation above and below this level.
Some stations have comparatively narrow distributions. Wexford Harbour, for example, has a noticeably smaller interquartile range than most other stations despite having a broader overall range. This likely reflects genuine local tidal characteristics.
The two most striking stations are Galway Port 2 and Kinvara–Unreferenced. Galway Port 2 has an exceptionally narrow distribution centred at approximately −1 m OD Malin. From the previous plots, this station also contains extremely few observations, so its boxplot should not be interpreted as representative of a normal tidal distribution.
More importantly, Kinvara–Unreferenced is clearly separated from the remainder of the network, with observations centred at approximately −2.5 m OD Malin and a very narrow range. Its distribution is inconsistent with the other stations and suggests a possible issue with the vertical datum, station metadata, or water-level measurements. This provides strong justification for investigating Kinvara separately before including it in modelling alongside the other stations.


Show code
water_level_summary <- da |>
  group_by(source, st_id, station_id) |>
  summarise(n = sum(!is.na(Water_Level_OD_Malin)),
    missing = sum(is.na(Water_Level_OD_Malin)),
    minimum = min(Water_Level_OD_Malin, na.rm = TRUE),
    q01 = quantile(Water_Level_OD_Malin, 0.01, na.rm = TRUE),
    q05 = quantile(Water_Level_OD_Malin, 0.05, na.rm = TRUE),
    median = median(Water_Level_OD_Malin, na.rm = TRUE),
    mean = mean(Water_Level_OD_Malin, na.rm = TRUE),
    q95 = quantile(Water_Level_OD_Malin, 0.95, na.rm = TRUE),
    q99 = quantile(Water_Level_OD_Malin, 0.99, na.rm = TRUE),
    maximum = max(Water_Level_OD_Malin, na.rm = TRUE),
    sd = sd(Water_Level_OD_Malin, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop")


da |>
  filter(!is.na(Water_Level_OD_Malin)) |>
  mutate(station_id = fct_reorder(station_id, Water_Level_OD_Malin, median, na.rm = TRUE)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = station_id, y = Water_Level_OD_Malin)) +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.shape = NA, linewidth = 0.7, width = 0.65) +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(title = "Observed Water-Level Range by Station", x = NULL, y = "Water level (m OD Malin)") +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(size = 16, face = "bold"),
    axis.title.x = element_text(size = 12),
    axis.text.x = element_text(size = 9),
    axis.text.y = element_text(size = 9),
    panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank())









This plot shows the distribution of observed water levels at each tide-gauge station and provides a useful comparison of the shape, location and spread of the water-level records across the network.
For most stations, the distributions have the expected bimodal or weakly bimodal shape associated with tidal observations. The two broad peaks reflect the tendency for observations to accumulate around low and high stages of the tidal cycle, with comparatively less time spent around intermediate water levels. Although the precise location and separation of these peaks varies among stations, most distributions occupy a broadly similar range and appear physically plausible.
A few stations stand out from the general pattern. Galway Port 2 has an extremely concentrated distribution, which is consistent with the earlier finding that this station contains very few observations. Its apparent distribution therefore cannot be considered representative of the normal tidal behaviour at the location. Tivoli Docks also has an unusual distribution, with a pronounced narrow peak and a broader component extending towards higher water levels. These stations are to be removed because they have fewer than three years of observations, so further examination of these distributions is not necessary at this stage.
The most striking anomaly is Kinvara–Unreferenced. Unlike almost every other station, it does not display the broad tidal distribution expected from a continuously sampled water-level record. Instead, there is a very sharp concentration of observations at approximately −2.5 to −2.7 m OD Malin, accompanied by a much smaller and more diffuse distribution extending towards higher water levels. This explains why Kinvara appeared so clearly separated from the other stations in the preceding boxplot.
Importantly, this suggests that the Kinvara issue is not simply that the entire tidal record has been shifted vertically by a constant datum offset. If that were the only problem, we would still expect to see a reasonably broad, tidal-shaped distribution, just centred at a different elevation. The very large spike instead suggests that a substantial proportion of observations are concentrated at or very close to one particular value.
That pattern could arise from several data issues, including a repeated placeholder or default value, periods when the gauge became effectively fixed at one measurement, values introduced during missing-data processing, or a change in the way the Kinvara observations were recorded. The smaller distribution extending away from the spike may represent a subset of the record in which the gauge was behaving normally.
Overall, most stations show distributions consistent with continuously varying tidal water levels, while Kinvara–Unreferenced is a clear outlier in both the location and shape of its distribution. Plotting Kinvara through time and separating its distributions by year should tell us whether the spike corresponds to a particular period of the record and whether there is a usable portion of the station data that can be retained.


Show code
da |>
  filter(!is.na(Water_Level_OD_Malin)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = Water_Level_OD_Malin)) +
  geom_histogram(aes(y = after_stat(density)), bins = 60, alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_density(linewidth = 0.7, na.rm = TRUE) +
  facet_wrap(~ station_id, scales = "free_y", ncol = 4) +
  labs(title = "Distribution of Observed Water Levels by Station", x = "Water level (m OD Malin)", y = "Density") +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(size = 16, face = "bold"),
    axis.title = element_text(size = 12),
    axis.text = element_text(size = 9),
    strip.text = element_text(size = 9),
    panel.spacing = unit(0.8, "lines"))









This year-by-year breakdown confirms that the unusual distribution observed for Kinvara–Unreferenced is persistent throughout the entire available record, rather than being caused by a single anomalous year or a short period of poor-quality observations.
From 2018 through 2024, each year shows a pronounced concentration of observations at approximately −2.5 m OD Malin. The frequency of observations at or very close to this value is much greater than at surrounding water levels, producing the large spike seen in the overall distribution. Although observations extend across a wider range of water levels, they do not form the broad, approximately bimodal tidal distributions expected at other stations.
The consistency of this feature across years is particularly important. If the unusual distribution were confined to one year, it might be possible to identify and remove a specific period of erroneous measurements while retaining the remainder of the station record. Instead, the same behaviour is present from the beginning to the end of the available Kinvara record. This suggests a systematic problem with the station data, rather than an isolated period of missingness or sensor malfunction.
There is consequently no clearly identifiable period within the available Kinvara record that can be considered representative of a normal continuous tidal time series. Kinvara–Unreferenced will therefore be excluded from the subsequent tidal analysis.


Show code
kinvara <- da |>
  filter(st_id == "Kinvara-Unreferenced", !is.na(Water_Level_OD_Malin))

kinvara |>
  mutate(year = year(time)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = Water_Level_OD_Malin)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 50) +
  facet_wrap(~ year, scales = "free_y", ncol = 4) +
  labs(title = "Kinvara Water-Level Distribution by Year", x = "Water level (m OD Malin)", y = "Number of observations") +
  theme_bw()

title: Exploring the Tide-Gauge Data
Exploring the Tide-Gauge Data
text:
Stations retained for analysis
The exploratory analysis above identified three criteria that determine whether a station is retained for the subsequent tidal analysis.
First, stations must have a minimum record span of three years. Second, the available observations must provide a sufficiently continuous and usable record; a record spanning three years or more is not considered sufficient if the observations are separated by substantial gaps that prevent the construction of the required analysis windows. Finally, stations with persistent anomalies in their observed water-level distributions are excluded where the available record cannot be considered representative of a normal tidal time series.
Applying these criteria results in five stations being excluded. Galway Port 2, Tivoli Docks and Bantry are excluded because they contain fewer than three years of available data. Roonagh Pier is excluded because, despite its elapsed record span exceeding three years, the observations do not form a sufficiently continuous record. Kinvara–Unreferenced is excluded because of the persistent anomalous water-level distribution identified throughout its available record.
Below is the final list of stations to be retained for analysis, followed by a table detailing the excluded stations and the reason for their exclusion.


Show code
station_coverage <- station_coverage |>
  mutate(
    include_analysis = case_when(
      record_years < MIN_RECORD_YEARS ~ FALSE,
      st_id == "RoonaghPier" ~ FALSE,
      st_id == "Kinvara-Unreferenced" ~ FALSE,
      TRUE ~ TRUE
    ),
    exclusion_reason = case_when(
      record_years < MIN_RECORD_YEARS ~ "Less than 3 years of available data",
      st_id == "RoonaghPier" ~ "Insufficient consecutive usable data due to a large gap in the record",
      st_id == "Kinvara-Unreferenced" ~ "Persistent anomalous water-level distribution",
      TRUE ~ NA_character_
    )
  )

included_stations <- station_coverage |>
  filter(include_analysis) |>
  arrange(source, station_id)

included_stations |>
  select(source, station_id, st_id, first_obs, last_obs, record_years, n_observations) |>
  knitr::kable(
    digits = 2,
    format = "html",
    format.args = list(big.mark = ",")
  ) |>
  kableExtra::kable_styling(
    full_width = TRUE,
    bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover", "condensed")
  ) |>
  kableExtra::scroll_box(

title: Modelling tidal features
text:
This analysis investigates how the estimated tidal features vary through time at GalwayPort. The tidal harmonic analysis provides estimates of seven tidal characteristics: Highest Astronomical Tide (HAT), Mean High Water Springs (MHWS), Mean High Water Neaps (MHWN), Mean Sea Level (MSL), Mean Low Water Neaps (MLWN), Mean Low Water Springs (MLWS), and Lowest Astronomical Tide (LAT). Rather than treating these characteristics as fixed quantities over the complete observational record, the preceding analysis estimated them repeatedly using rolling time windows, allowing their temporal behaviour to be examined.


Show code
## Packages
library(arrow)
library(tidyverse)
library(patchwork)
library(TideHarmonics)
library(INLA)
here::i_am("index.qmd")
source(here::here("scripts", "_functions.R"))
theme_set(theme_bw() + theme(legend.position = "right", legend.direction = "vertical"))


## Full dataset
fl <- here::here("rds", sprintf("features-%s.rds", params$station))
da <- readRDS(fl)

## Set ther levels for constituents
const_levels <- c("HAT","MHWS", "MHWN", "MSL", "MLWN", "MLWS","LAT")
## Select the windown interval
ws <- "y_3"
## Define years to predict
yrs <- range(da$year_mid) + c(-10, 10)
yrs_seq <- seq(yrs[1], yrs[2])

## Split by constituent and create a list
db <- da |>
    filter(window_size == ws) |>
    split(~constituent)

## Arrange and complete with more years
db <- imap(db, \(x, nm) {
    x |>
        arrange(year_mid) |>
        complete(year_mid = yrs_seq, fill = list(constituent = nm)) |>
        mutate(constituent = fct_relevel(constituent, const_levels),
            id = seq_along(year_mid), id2 = id, id3 = id)
})

title: Modelling tidal features
text:
Time series
The following figure shows the 3-year rolling-window estimates of the seven tidal features at Galway Port from 2009 to 2022. Each point represents the tidal characteristic estimated from a three-year period, positioned at the midpoint year of that window.
The tidal features show clear separation, ranging from HAT at approximately 3 m OD Malin to LAT at approximately −3 m OD Malin, with MSL remaining close to zero.
The upper tidal levels, particularly HAT and MHWS, generally decline from the earlier part of the series before becoming comparatively stable in the later years. A corresponding change can be seen in the lower tidal levels: MLWS and LAT become less negative through the middle of the record, indicating some narrowing of the tidal range. MHWN and MLWN show smaller changes, while MSL exhibits only modest fluctuations around a relatively stable level.
There also appears to be temporal dependence in the trajectories, with neighbouring rolling-window estimates generally similar to one another rather than fluctuating independently. Some of this smoothness is expected because consecutive 3-year windows overlap and share two years of observations. Nevertheless, the presence of gradual changes through time motivates considering models that can represent both systematic trends and additional temporal structure.
Overall, this exploratory analysis suggests that the tidal features are not necessarily well represented by a single constant value through time, while the nature and magnitude of the temporal variation differ between features.


Show code
db |>
    bind_rows() |>
    filter(!is.na(value)) |>
    ggplot(aes(x = year_mid, y = value, color = constituent)) +
    geom_line() +
    geom_point() +
    scale_x_continuous(breaks = scales::pretty_breaks(n = 20))

title: Calculating tidal levels for AranmoreIsland-Leabgarrow
text:
The aim of this document is to explore tide-level data from the Marine Institute (MI) and the Office of Public Works (OPW). The final result should be to obtain the tidal levels for each station in Ireland where MI/OPW has available data.





Code

library(tidyverse)

## Full dataset
fl <- here::here("data", "merged_tide_gauge_data", "iteration_a_qc1")

## Station-specific start dates

  "Inishmore" = "2016-01-01",
  "Sligo" = "2018-01-01",
  "SkerriesHarbour" = "2013-01-01"
)

## Filter for station
db <- da |>
  filter(st_id == params$station) |>
  mutate(year = year(time), .before = "station_id") |>
  mutate(QC_Flag = NULL, sea_level = Water_Level_OD_Malin, Water_Level_OD_Malin = NULL) |>
  arrange(time) |>
  collect()

## Apply station-specific start date where required
if (params$station %in% names(station_start_dates)) {

    filter(time >= as.POSIXct(station_start_dates[[params$station]], tz = "UTC"))
}


## Save the name for posterior use

## Save lat/lon for posterior use

lon <- unique(db$longitude)

record_end   <- max(db$time, na.rm = TRUE)

record_days <- as.numeric(difftime(record_end, record_start, units = "days"))

record_years <- record_days / 365.25

## Minimum record length used in the tidal analysis
MIN_RECORD_YEARS <- 3

## This is the sampling time, completed and standardised to 10 minutes
db_comp <- db |>
    select(-c(year, dtime)) |>
    mutate(time_rounded = floor_date(time, "10 min")) |>

    summarise(
        sea_level = mean(sea_level, na.rm = TRUE),
        n_obs = n(),
        n_na = sum(is.na(sea_level)),
        .groups = "drop"
    ) |>
    rename(time = time_rounded) |>
    distinct(time, .keep_all = TRUE) |>
    arrange(time) |>
    mutate(
        sea_level = ifelse(is.nan(sea_level), NA_real_, sea_level),
        dtime = as.numeric(difftime(time, lag(time), units = "mins"))

## Define the period to use for the tidal analysis
##
## Stations must have at least 3 years of data to be included.
## Stations with less than 3 years are excluded.

if (record_years < 3) {
    stop(sprintf("%s has only %.2f years of data and is excluded from the tidal analysis.", st_id, record_years))
}

## Identify complete calendar years

complete_years <- db_comp |>
    mutate(year = year(time), month = month(time)) |>
    group_by(year) |>
    summarise(
        min_month = min(month),
        max_month = max(month),
        n_months = n_distinct(month),
        .groups = "drop"
    ) |>
    filter(min_month == 1, max_month == 12, n_months == 12) |>
    arrange(year)

## Check that at least one complete calendar year exists
if (nrow(complete_years) == 0) {
    stop(sprintf("%s has no complete calendar years available for tidal analysis.", st_id))
}

## First and last complete calendar years
year_first <- min(complete_years$year)
year_last <- max(complete_years$year)
year_all <- year_first:year_last



## Check that the complete-year analysis period contains at least 3 years

if (length(year_all) < 3) {
    stop(sprintf(paste0("%s has %.2f years of raw data, but fewer than 3 complete ", "calendar years are available after restricting the analysis period."), st_id, record_years))
}



## Restrict to complete-year period
db_comp <- db_comp |>
    filter(year(time) >= year_first, year(time) <= year_last) |>
    arrange(time)

dtab_comp <- db_comp |>
    summarise(dmin = min(time), dmax = max(time))

## Check that each proposed window contains usable observations
## Some stations may span several calendar years but contain little or no
## usable sea-level data within an individual rolling window. Remove such
## windows before fitting the TideHarmonics model.

seq_checked <- vector(mode = "list", length = length(seq))
names(seq_checked) <- names(seq)


for (i in seq_along(seq)) {
    valid_windows <- list()
    for (j in seq_along(seq[[i]])) {
        n1 <- names(seq)[[i]]
        n2 <- names(seq[[i]])[[j]]
        
        ## Define calendar-year limits for this window
        t1 <- make_datetime(year = min(seq[[i]][[j]]))
        t2 <- make_datetime(year = max(seq[[i]][[j]]), month = 12, day = 31, hour = 23, min = 50)
        
        ## Extract data for this window
        db_window <- db_comp |>
            filter(time >= t1, time <= t2)
        
        ## Count usable sea-level observations
        n_non_na <- sum(!is.na(db_window$sea_level))

        ## Keep only windows containing usable observations
        if (n_non_na > 0) {
            valid_windows[[n2]] <- seq[[i]][[j]]
        } 
    }

    ## Store valid windows for this window size
    seq_checked[[i]] <- valid_windows
}



## Remove window-size groups containing no valid windows
seq <- seq_checked[lengths(seq_checked) > 0]


## Stop if no usable windows remain
if (length(seq) == 0) {
    stop(sprintf("No usable tidal-analysis windows remain for station %s.", st_id))
}

## Create a list to hold model results
res <- vector(mode = "list",length = length(seq))
names(res) <- names(seq)


for (i in seq_along(res)) {
    res[[i]] <- vector(mode = "list", length = length(seq[[i]]))
    names(res[[i]]) <- names(seq[[i]])
}



## Fit all valid windows
for (i in seq_along(res)) {
    for (j in seq_along(res[[i]])) {

        n1 <- names(seq)[[i]]
        n2 <- names(seq[[i]])[[j]]
        
        ## Define calendar-year limits
        t1 <- make_datetime(year = min(seq[[i]][[j]]))
        t2 <- make_datetime(year = max(seq[[i]][[j]]), month = 12, day = 31, hour = 23, min = 50)

        ## Extract data for this fitting window
        db_window <- db_comp |>
            filter(time >= t1, time <= t2)
        
        ## Model file
        fl <- here::here("rds", sprintf("fit-%s-%s-%s.rds", n1, n2, st_id))

        ## Fit model if it has not already been saved
        if (!file.exists(fl)) {
            res[[i]][[j]] <- fit_th(x = db_window$sea_level, dto = db_window$time, pred = FALSE)
            saveRDS(res[[i]][[j]], fl)

        } else {
           res[[i]][[j]] <- readRDS(fl)
        }
    }
}


The harmonic model was fitted for three different time intervals (or time windows):

3 years
5 years
15 years.






K1, O1, M2, and S2 are the main tidal constituents because they represent the dominant astronomical forcing mechanisms and typically have the largest amplitudes.

Semi-diurnal constituents (2 cycles per day):

M2 (Principal lunar semi-diurnal): The largest tidal constituent in most places. Period = 12.42 hours. Caused by the moon’s gravitational pull as Earth rotates beneath it.
S2 (Principal solar semi-diurnal): Second largest semi-diurnal constituent. Period = 12.00 hours. Caused by the sun’s gravitational pull.

Diurnal constituents (1 cycle per day):

K1 (Lunisolar diurnal): Largest diurnal constituent. Period = 23.93 hours. Results from the declination of the moon and sun.
O1 (Principal lunar diurnal): Second largest diurnal constituent. Period = 25.82 hours. Due to lunar declination effects.


Why these four matters:

Largest amplitudes: They typically account for 70-90% of tidal variance
Physical significance:

M2 & S2 create spring-neap cycles (14-day variation)
K1 & O1 create diurnal inequality (different heights of successive high/low tides)

Tidal classification: The form factor (K1+O1)/(M2+S2) uses these to classify whether tides are semi-diurnal, diurnal, or mixed
Coastal features: MHWS, MLWS, etc. are primarily defined by M2 and S2



Code
## Extract constituent amplitudes
constituent_amps <- map(res, \(x) map(x, \(y) {
  coefs <- y$coefficients
  tibble(
    K1 = sqrt(coefs["K1_C"]^2 + coefs["K1_S"]^2),
    O1 = sqrt(coefs["O1_C"]^2 + coefs["O1_S"]^2),
    M2 = sqrt(coefs["M2_C"]^2 + coefs["M2_S"]^2),
    S2 = sqrt(coefs["S2_C"]^2 + coefs["S2_S"]^2)
  )
})) |>
  imap_dfr(function(window_list, window_name) {
    imap_dfr(window_list, function(amps, year_range) {
      amps |>
        mutate(window_size = window_name, year_range = year_range, .before = 1)
    })
  }) |>
  mutate(
    n_years = as.integer(str_extract(window_size, "\\d+")),
    year_end = as.integer(str_extract(year_range, "(?<=y)\\d+")),
    year_start = as.integer(str_extract(year_range, "\\d+$")),
    year_mid = (year_start + year_end) / 2
  ) |>
  pivot_longer(cols = c(K1, O1, M2, S2), names_to = "constituent", values_to = "amplitude")

## Plot
## Extract the last window size as the full-record reference
ly <- constituent_amps$window_size |> tail(1)

amps_ref <- constituent_amps |>
    filter(window_size == ly) |>
    select(constituent, amplitude)

## Create better labels for window_size
window_labels <- c("y_3" = "3 years range",  "y_5" = "5 years range")

## Data used for rolling-window comparison
plot_data <- constituent_amps |>
    filter(window_size != ly)

## Plot only when there is at least one rolling window available
if (nrow(plot_data) > 0) {

    plot_data |>
        ggplot(aes(x = make_datetime(year_mid), y = amplitude)) +
        geom_hline(data = amps_ref, aes(yintercept = amplitude, linetype = "Full dataset"), color = "red", alpha = 0.7) +
        geom_line() +
        geom_point() +
        facet_grid(constituent ~ window_size, scales = "free_y", labeller = labeller(window_size = window_labels)) +
        scale_x_datetime(date_breaks = "2 year", date_minor_breaks = "1 year", date_labels = "%Y") +
        scale_linetype_manual(name = "Reference", values = c("Full dataset" = "dashed")) +
        labs(x = "Midpoint Year", y = "Amplitude (m)", title = "Tidal Constituent Amplitudes Over Time")

} else {

    cat("Only one analysis window is available for this station. ", "A rolling-window comparison plot is therefore not shown.")
}












The form factor is calculated by
\[(K1+O1)/(M2+S2)\]
and it classifies tides as:

< 0.25: Semi-diurnal
0.25-1.5: Mixed, mainly semi-diurnal
1.5-3.0: Mixed, mainly diurnal
> 3.0: Diurnal

    imap_dfr(function(window_list, window_name) {
        imap_dfr(window_list, function(fval, year_range) {
            tibble(window_size = window_name, year_range = year_range, fval = fval)

Tidal levels (or features) are defined as:

HAT (Highest Astronomical Tide) = maximum predicted astronomical tide over the reference prediction period
MSL (Mean Sea Level) = mean of the time series (or the constant/mean term in the model)
MHWS (Mean High Water Springs) = MSL + M2_amp + S2_amp
MHWN (Mean High Water Neaps) = MSL + M2_amp - S2_amp
MLWN (Mean Low Water Neaps) = MSL - M2_amp + S2_amp
MLWS (Mean Low Water Springs) = MSL - M2_amp - S2_amp
LAT (Lowest Astronomical Tide) = minimum predicted astronomical tide over the reference prediction period

Where:

M2 = principal lunar semi-diurnal (largest constituent)
S2 = principal solar semi-diurnal

Springs occur when M2 and S2 are in phase (add together), creating the highest highs and lowest lows.
Neaps occur when M2 and S2 are out of phase (subtract), creating smaller tidal ranges.


Code
hat_lat_data <- imap_dfr(res, function(window_list, window_name) {
    imap_dfr(window_list, function(fit, year_range) {
        lat_hat_file <- here::here("rds", "lat-hat", sprintf("lat-hat-%s-%s-%s.rds", window_name, year_range, st_id))
        ## Default: no calculation failure
        lat_hat_error <- NA_character_

        ## Read existing result or calculate a new one

        if (file.exists(lat_hat_file)) {
            lat_hat <- readRDS(lat_hat_file)
        } else {
            lat_hat <- tryCatch(calculate_lat_hat(fit = fit), error = function(e) {
                    lat_hat_error <<- conditionMessage(e)
                    cat(sprintf(paste0("WARNING: LAT/HAT calculation failed for ", "%s | %s | %s\n", "Reason: %s\n"),
                            st_id, window_name, year_range, lat_hat_error))

                    tibble(constituent = c("LAT", "HAT"), value = c(NA_real_, NA_real_))
                }
            )
        }

        
        ## Check HAT/LAT values
        ##
        ## This is deliberately a very generous threshold. It is intended only
        ## to identify catastrophic numerical/extrapolation failures such as
        ## HAT/LAT values of hundreds or millions of metres.
        ##
        ## It should not affect plausible tidal estimates.

        MAX_ABS_TIDAL_LEVEL <- 20
        lat_value <- lat_hat |>
            filter(constituent == "LAT") |>
            pull(value)
        hat_value <- lat_hat |>
            filter(constituent == "HAT") |>
            pull(value)
        
        ## Determine whether the calculated values are numerically plausible
        invalid_lat_hat <- FALSE
        if (length(lat_value) != 1L || length(hat_value) != 1L) {
            invalid_lat_hat <- TRUE
            lat_hat_error <- paste0("LAT/HAT calculation returned an unexpected number of values.")

        } else if (!is.finite(lat_value) || !is.finite(hat_value)) {
            invalid_lat_hat <- TRUE
            lat_hat_error <- paste0("LAT/HAT calculation returned non-finite values.")

        } else if (abs(lat_value) > MAX_ABS_TIDAL_LEVEL || abs(hat_value) > MAX_ABS_TIDAL_LEVEL) {
            invalid_lat_hat <- TRUE
            lat_hat_error <- sprintf(paste0("Numerically implausible LAT/HAT values detected ", "(LAT = %.3f m, HAT = %.3f m)."),  lat_value, hat_value)

        } else if (lat_value >= hat_value) {
            invalid_lat_hat <- TRUE
            lat_hat_error <- sprintf(paste0("Invalid LAT/HAT ordering ", "(LAT = %.3f m, HAT = %.3f m)."), lat_value, hat_value)
        }

        ## If the LAT/HAT values are invalid, replace them with NA
        ## The tidal harmonic fit itself is retained. Only the unreliable
        ## astronomical extremes are removed.
        if (invalid_lat_hat) {
            cat(sprintf(paste0("WARNING: Rejecting LAT/HAT for ", "%s | %s | %s\n", "Reason: %s\n"),
                    st_id, window_name, year_range, lat_hat_error))
            lat_hat <- lat_hat |>
                mutate(value = NA_real_)

        } else {
            ## Save only valid LAT/HAT calculations
            if (!file.exists(lat_hat_file)) {
                saveRDS(lat_hat, lat_hat_file)
            }
        }
        
        ## Format output
        lat_hat |>
            select(constituent, value) |>
            mutate(window_size = window_name, year_range = year_range, lat_hat_error = lat_hat_error, .before = 1)
    })

title: Calculating tidal levels for AranmoreIsland-Leabgarrow
text: The aim of this document is to explore tide-level data from the Marine Institute (MI) and the Office of Public Works (OPW). The final result should be to obtain the tidal levels for each station in Ireland where MI/OPW has available data.

title: Calculating tidal levels for AranmoreIsland-Leabgarrow

Code
## Packages
library(arrow)
library(tidyverse)
library(patchwork)
library(TideHarmonics)
here::i_am("index.qmd")
source(here::here("scripts", "_functions.R"))
theme_set(theme_bw() + theme(legend.position = "right", legend.direction = "vertical"))


## Full dataset
fl <- here::here("data", "merged_tide_gauge_data", "iteration_a_qc1")
da <- open_dataset(fl, format="parquet")

## Station-specific start dates
station_start_dates <- c(
  "Inishmore" = "2016-01-01",
  "Sligo" = "2018-01-01",
  "SkerriesHarbour" = "2013-01-01"
)

## Filter for station
db <- da |>
  filter(st_id == params$station) |>
  mutate(year = year(time), .before = "station_id") |>
  mutate(QC_Flag = NULL, sea_level = Water_Level_OD_Malin, Water_Level_OD_Malin = NULL) |>
  arrange(time) |>
  collect()

## Apply station-specific start date where required
if (params$station %in% names(station_start_dates)) {
  db <- db |>
    filter(time >= as.POSIXct(station_start_dates[[params$station]], tz = "UTC"))
}


## Save the name for posterior use
station_id <- unique(db$station_id)
st_id <- gsub(" ", "", station_id)
## Save lat/lon for posterior use
lat <- unique(db$latitude)
lon <- unique(db$longitude)

## Check dates
dtab <- db |> summarise(dmin = min(time), dmax = max(time))



## Length of the actual available record

record_start <- min(db$time, na.rm = TRUE)
record_end   <- max(db$time, na.rm = TRUE)

record_days <- as.numeric(difftime(record_end, record_start, units = "days"))

record_years <- record_days / 365.25

## Minimum record length used in the tidal analysis
MIN_RECORD_YEARS <- 3

## This is the sampling time, completed and standardised to 10 minutes
db_comp <- db |>
    select(-c(year, dtime)) |>
    mutate(time_rounded = floor_date(time, "10 min")) |>
    complete(time_rounded = seq(min(time_rounded), max(time_rounded), by = "10 min")) |>
    group_by(time_rounded) |>
    summarise(
        sea_level = mean(sea_level, na.rm = TRUE),
        n_obs = n(),
        n_na = sum(is.na(sea_level)),
        .groups = "drop"
    ) |>
    rename(time = time_rounded) |>
    distinct(time, .keep_all = TRUE) |>
    arrange(time) |>
    mutate(
        sea_level = ifelse(is.nan(sea_level), NA_real_, sea_level),
        dtime = as.numeric(difftime(time, lag(time), units = "mins"))
    )

## Define the period to use for the tidal analysis
##
## Stations must have at least 3 years of data to be included.
## Stations with less than 3 years are excluded.

if (record_years < 3) {
    stop(sprintf("%s has only %.2f years of data and is excluded from the tidal analysis.", st_id, record_years))
}

## Identify complete calendar years

complete_years <- db_comp |>
    mutate(year = year(time), month = month(time)) |>
    group_by(year) |>
    summarise(
        min_month = min(month),
        max_month = max(month),
        n_months = n_distinct(month),
        .groups = "drop"
    ) |>
    filter(min_month == 1, max_month == 12, n_months == 12) |>
    arrange(year)

## Check that at least one complete calendar year exists
if (nrow(complete_years) == 0) {
    stop(sprintf("%s has no complete calendar years available for tidal analysis.", st_id))
}

## First and last complete calendar years
year_first <- min(complete_years$year)
year_last <- max(complete_years$year)
year_all <- year_first:year_last



## Check that the complete-year analysis period contains at least 3 years

if (length(year_all) < 3) {
    stop(sprintf(paste0("%s has %.2f years of raw data, but fewer than 3 complete ", "calendar years are available after restricting the analysis period."), st_id, record_years))
}



## Restrict to complete-year period
db_comp <- db_comp |>
    filter(year(time) >= year_first, year(time) <= year_last) |>
    arrange(time)

dtab_comp <- db_comp |>
    summarise(dmin = min(time), dmax = max(time))


To standardise the sample interval, a sampling interval is defined, and all the data was adjuted to fit between this interval.
This was determined using the first and last “full years” of the dataset, i.e., the first and final years where data is available for all the 12 months. In this case, the first full year is 2009, and the last full year is 2023, giving in total a range of 15 years.
The final dataset has then 788832 observations, within a 10 minute sample interval:

The first observation is on 2009-01-01
The last observation is on 2023-12-31 23:50:00

## Create the fitting windows
k <- c(3, 5, length(year_all))

## Avoid duplicate intervals
##
## For example, if there are exactly 5 years available then:
## 5-year window == full-record window so only one copy is retained.
k <- unique(k)

## Create rolling windows
seq <- map(k, \(x) seq_win(year_all, k = x, step = 1))

names(seq) <- sprintf("y_%s", k)



## Name individual year windows
for (i in seq_along(seq)) {

    names(seq[[i]]) <- sprintf("y%s_%s", sapply(seq[[i]], \(x) max(x)), sapply(seq[[i]], \(x) min(x)))
}



## Display fitting windows as a tidy table

window_table <- imap_dfr(seq, \(window_list, window_name) {
        imap_dfr(window_list, \(years, window_id) {
                tibble(
                    window_size = window_name,
                    year_range = window_id,
                    first_year = min(years),
                    last_year = max(years),
                    n_years = length(years))
            }
        )
    }
)

## Some stations may span several calendar years but contain little or no
## usable sea-level data within an individual rolling window. Remove such
## windows before fitting the TideHarmonics model.

seq_checked <- vector(mode = "list", length = length(seq))

    valid_windows <- list()
    for (j in seq_along(seq[[i]])) {
        n1 <- names(seq)[[i]]
        n2 <- names(seq[[i]])[[j]]
        
        ## Define calendar-year limits for this window
        t1 <- make_datetime(year = min(seq[[i]][[j]]))
        t2 <- make_datetime(year = max(seq[[i]][[j]]), month = 12, day = 31, hour = 23, min = 50)
        
        ## Extract data for this window
        db_window <- db_comp |>
            filter(time >= t1, time <= t2)
        
        ## Count usable sea-level observations
        n_non_na <- sum(!is.na(db_window$sea_level))

        ## Keep only windows containing usable observations
        if (n_non_na > 0) {
            valid_windows[[n2]] <- seq[[i]][[j]]
        } 
    }

    ## Store valid windows for this window size
    seq_checked[[i]] <- valid_windows
}



## Remove window-size groups containing no valid windows
seq <- seq_checked[lengths(seq_checked) > 0]


## Stop if no usable windows remain
if (length(seq) == 0) {
    stop(sprintf("No usable tidal-analysis windows remain for station %s.", st_id))
}

## Create a list to hold model results
res <- vector(mode = "list",length = length(seq))
names(res) <- names(seq)


for (i in seq_along(res)) {
    res[[i]] <- vector(mode = "list", length = length(seq[[i]]))
    names(res[[i]]) <- names(seq[[i]])
}



## Fit all valid windows
for (i in seq_along(res)) {
    for (j in seq_along(res[[i]])) {

        n1 <- names(seq)[[i]]
        n2 <- names(seq[[i]])[[j]]
        
        ## Define calendar-year limits
        t1 <- make_datetime(year = min(seq[[i]][[j]]))
        t2 <- make_datetime(year = max(seq[[i]][[j]]), month = 12, day = 31, hour = 23, min = 50)

        ## Extract data for this fitting window
        db_window <- db_comp |>
            filter(time >= t1, time <= t2)
        
        ## Model file
        fl <- here::here("rds", sprintf("fit-%s-%s-%s.rds", n1, n2, st_id))

        ## Fit model if it has not already been saved
        if (!file.exists(fl)) {
            res[[i]][[j]] <- fit_th(x = db_window$sea_level, dto = db_window$time, pred = FALSE)
            saveRDS(res[[i]][[j]], fl)

        } else {
           res[[i]][[j]] <- readRDS(fl)
        }
    }
}


The harmonic model was fitted for three different time intervals (or time windows):

3 years
5 years
15 years.






K1, O1, M2, and S2 are the main tidal constituents because they represent the dominant astronomical forcing mechanisms and typically have the largest amplitudes.

Semi-diurnal constituents (2 cycles per day):

M2 (Principal lunar semi-diurnal): The largest tidal constituent in most places. Period = 12.42 hours. Caused by the moon’s gravitational pull as Earth rotates beneath it.
S2 (Principal solar semi-diurnal): Second largest semi-diurnal constituent. Period = 12.00 hours. Caused by the sun’s gravitational pull.

Diurnal constituents (1 cycle per day):

K1 (Lunisolar diurnal): Largest diurnal constituent. Period = 23.93 hours. Results from the declination of the moon and sun.
O1 (Principal lunar diurnal): Second largest diurnal constituent. Period = 25.82 hours. Due to lunar declination effects.


Why these four matters:

Largest amplitudes: They typically account for 70-90% of tidal variance
Physical significance:

M2 & S2 create spring-neap cycles (14-day variation)
K1 & O1 create diurnal inequality (different heights of successive high/low tides)

Tidal classification: The form factor (K1+O1)/(M2+S2) uses these to classify whether tides are semi-diurnal, diurnal, or mixed
Coastal features: MHWS, MLWS, etc. are primarily defined by M2 and S2



Code
## Extract constituent amplitudes
constituent_amps <- map(res, \(x) map(x, \(y) {
  coefs <- y$coefficients
  tibble(
    K1 = sqrt(coefs["K1_C"]^2 + coefs["K1_S"]^2),
    O1 = sqrt(coefs["O1_C"]^2 + coefs["O1_S"]^2),
    M2 = sqrt(coefs["M2_C"]^2 + coefs["M2_S"]^2),

Tidal levels (or features) are defined as:

HAT (Highest Astronomical Tide) = maximum predicted astronomical tide over the reference prediction period
MSL (Mean Sea Level) = mean of the time series (or the constant/mean term in the model)
MHWS (Mean High Water Springs) = MSL + M2_amp + S2_amp
MHWN (Mean High Water Neaps) = MSL + M2_amp - S2_amp
MLWN (Mean Low Water Neaps) = MSL - M2_amp + S2_amp
MLWS (Mean Low Water Springs) = MSL - M2_amp - S2_amp
LAT (Lowest Astronomical Tide) = minimum predicted astronomical tide over the reference prediction period

Where:

M2 = principal lunar semi-diurnal (largest constituent)
S2 = principal solar semi-diurnal

Springs occur when M2 and S2 are in phase (add together), creating the highest highs and lowest lows.
Neaps occur when M2 and S2 are out of phase (subtract), creating smaller tidal ranges.


Code
hat_lat_data <- imap_dfr(res, function(window_list, window_name) {
    imap_dfr(window_list, function(fit, year_range) {
        lat_hat_file <- here::here("rds", "lat-hat", sprintf("lat-hat-%s-%s-%s.rds", window_name, year_range, st_id))
        ## Default: no calculation failure
        lat_hat_error <- NA_character_

        ## Read existing result or calculate a new one

        if (file.exists(lat_hat_file)) {
            lat_hat <- readRDS(lat_hat_file)
        } else {
            lat_hat <- tryCatch(calculate_lat_hat(fit = fit), error = function(e) {
                    lat_hat_error <<- conditionMessage(e)
                    cat(sprintf(paste0("WARNING: LAT/HAT calculation failed for ", "%s | %s | %s\n", "Reason: %s\n"),
                            st_id, window_name, year_range, lat_hat_error))

                    tibble(constituent = c("LAT", "HAT"), value = c(NA_real_, NA_real_))
                }
            )
        }

        
        ## Check HAT/LAT values
        ##
        ## This is deliberately a very generous threshold. It is intended only
        ## to identify catastrophic numerical/extrapolation failures such as
        ## HAT/LAT values of hundreds or millions of metres.
        ##
        ## It should not affect plausible tidal estimates.

        MAX_ABS_TIDAL_LEVEL <- 20
        lat_value <- lat_hat |>
            filter(constituent == "LAT") |>
            pull(value)
        hat_value <- lat_hat |>
            filter(constituent == "HAT") |>
            pull(value)
        
        ## Determine whether the calculated values are numerically plausible
        invalid_lat_hat <- FALSE
        if (length(lat_value) != 1L || length(hat_value) != 1L) {
            invalid_lat_hat <- TRUE
            lat_hat_error <- paste0("LAT/HAT calculation returned an unexpected number of values.")

        } else if (!is.finite(lat_value) || !is.finite(hat_value)) {
            invalid_lat_hat <- TRUE
            lat_hat_error <- paste0("LAT/HAT calculation returned non-finite values.")

        } else if (abs(lat_value) > MAX_ABS_TIDAL_LEVEL || abs(hat_value) > MAX_ABS_TIDAL_LEVEL) {
            invalid_lat_hat <- TRUE
            lat_hat_error <- sprintf(paste0("Numerically implausible LAT/HAT values detected ", "(LAT = %.3f m, HAT = %.3f m)."),  lat_value, hat_value)

        } else if (lat_value >= hat_value) {
            invalid_lat_hat <- TRUE
            lat_hat_error <- sprintf(paste0("Invalid LAT/HAT ordering ", "(LAT = %.3f m, HAT = %.3f m)."), lat_value, hat_value)
        }

        ## If the LAT/HAT values are invalid, replace them with NA
        ## The tidal harmonic fit itself is retained. Only the unreliable
        ## astronomical extremes are removed.
        if (invalid_lat_hat) {
            cat(sprintf(paste0("WARNING: Rejecting LAT/HAT for ", "%s | %s | %s\n", "Reason: %s\n"),
                    st_id, window_name, year_range, lat_hat_error))
            lat_hat <- lat_hat |>
                mutate(value = NA_real_)

        } else {
            ## Save only valid LAT/HAT calculations
            if (!file.exists(lat_hat_file)) {
                saveRDS(lat_hat, lat_hat_file)
            }
        }
        
        ## Format output
        lat_hat |>
            select(constituent, value) |>
            mutate(window_size = window_name, year_range = year_range, lat_hat_error = lat_hat_error, .before = 1)
    })
}) |>

title: Calculating tidal levels for BallyglassHarbour
text:
The aim of this document is to explore tide-level data from the Marine Institute (MI) and the Office of Public Works (OPW). The final result should be to obtain the tidal levels for each station in Ireland where MI/OPW has available data.





Code
## Packages
library(arrow)
library(tidyverse)
library(patchwork)
library(TideHarmonics)
here::i_am("index.qmd")
source(here::here("scripts", "_functions.R"))
theme_set(theme_bw() + theme(legend.position = "right", legend.direction = "vertical"))


## Full dataset
fl <- here::here("data", "merged_tide_gauge_data", "iteration_a_qc1")
da <- open_dataset(fl, format="parquet")

## Station-specific start dates
station_start_dates <- c(
  "Inishmore" = "2016-01-01",
  "Sligo" = "2018-01-01",
  "SkerriesHarbour" = "2013-01-01"
)

## Filter for station
db <- da |>
  filter(st_id == params$station) |>
  mutate(year = year(time), .before = "station_id") |>
  mutate(QC_Flag = NULL, sea_level = Water_Level_OD_Malin, Water_Level_OD_Malin = NULL) |>
  arrange(time) |>
  collect()

## Apply station-specific start date where required
if (params$station %in% names(station_start_dates)) {
  db <- db |>
    filter(time >= as.POSIXct(station_start_dates[[params$station]], tz = "UTC"))
}


## Save the name for posterior use
station_id <- unique(db$station_id)
st_id <- gsub(" ", "", station_id)
## Save lat/lon for posterior use
lat <- unique(db$latitude)
lon <- unique(db$longitude)

## Check dates
dtab <- db |> summarise(dmin = min(time), dmax = max(time))



## Length of the actual available record

record_start <- min(db$time, na.rm = TRUE)
record_end   <- max(db$time, na.rm = TRUE)

record_days <- as.numeric(difftime(record_end, record_start, units = "days"))

record_years <- record_days / 365.25

## Minimum record length used in the tidal analysis
MIN_RECORD_YEARS <- 3


This document examines the data for BallyglassHarbour, where:

The total number of observations is 1255857
The first observation was recorded on 2008-04-30 20:06:00
The last observation was recorded on 2024-10-03 11:30:00

The figure below shows the number of observations per year.


Code
## Count time series
db |>
    count(year) |>
    ggplot(aes(x = year, y = n)) +
    geom_line() +
    scale_x_continuous(breaks = scales::pretty_breaks(n = 10)) +
    labs(x = "Year", y = "Count", title = "Number of observations per year")









The full dataset is shown in the first panel below, while the second panel shows a random monthly variation, to check the tidal variability.


Code
## Full range
p1 <- db |>
    ggplot(aes(time, sea_level)) +
    geom_line() +
    scale_x_datetime(date_breaks = "2 years", date_minor_breaks = "1 year", date_labels = "%Y") +
    labs(title = sprintf("%s to %s", dtab$dmin, dtab$dmax), x = "Year", y = "Seal level")

dtab <- dtab |>
    mutate(smin = db |> slice_head(n = 5 * 90 * 24) |> pull(time) |> min(), smax = db |> slice_head(n = 5 * 90 * 24) |> pull(time) |> max())

p2 <- db |>
    filter(time >= dtab$smin, time <= dtab$smax) |>

        n2 <- names(seq[[i]])[[j]]
        
        ## Define calendar-year limits for this window
        t1 <- make_datetime(year = min(seq[[i]][[j]]))
        t2 <- make_datetime(year = max(seq[[i]][[j]]), month = 12, day = 31, hour = 23, min = 50)

K1, O1, M2, and S2 are the main tidal constituents because they represent the dominant astronomical forcing mechanisms and typically have the largest amplitudes.

Semi-diurnal constituents (2 cycles per day):

M2 (Principal lunar semi-diurnal): The largest tidal constituent in most places. Period = 12.42 hours. Caused by the moon’s gravitational pull as Earth rotates beneath it.
S2 (Principal solar semi-diurnal): Second largest semi-diurnal constituent. Period = 12.00 hours. Caused by the sun’s gravitational pull.

Diurnal constituents (1 cycle per day):

K1 (Lunisolar diurnal): Largest diurnal constituent. Period = 23.93 hours. Results from the declination of the moon and sun.
O1 (Principal lunar diurnal): Second largest diurnal constituent. Period = 25.82 hours. Due to lunar declination effects.


Why these four matters:

Largest amplitudes: They typically account for 70-90% of tidal variance
Physical significance:

M2 & S2 create spring-neap cycles (14-day variation)
K1 & O1 create diurnal inequality (different heights of successive high/low tides)

Tidal classification: The form factor (K1+O1)/(M2+S2) uses these to classify whether tides are semi-diurnal, diurnal, or mixed
Coastal features: MHWS, MLWS, etc. are primarily defined by M2 and S2

Tidal levels (or features) are defined as:

HAT (Highest Astronomical Tide) = maximum predicted astronomical tide over the reference prediction period
MSL (Mean Sea Level) = mean of the time series (or the constant/mean term in the model)
MHWS (Mean High Water Springs) = MSL + M2_amp + S2_amp
MHWN (Mean High Water Neaps) = MSL + M2_amp - S2_amp
MLWN (Mean Low Water Neaps) = MSL - M2_amp + S2_amp
MLWS (Mean Low Water Springs) = MSL - M2_amp - S2_amp
LAT (Lowest Astronomical Tide) = minimum predicted astronomical tide over the reference prediction period

Where:

M2 = principal lunar semi-diurnal (largest constituent)
S2 = principal solar semi-diurnal

Springs occur when M2 and S2 are in phase (add together), creating the highest highs and lowest lows.
Neaps occur when M2 and S2 are out of phase (subtract), creating smaller tidal ranges.

hat_lat_data <- imap_dfr(res, function(window_list, window_name) {
    imap_dfr(window_list, function(fit, year_range) {
        lat_hat_file <- here::here("rds", "lat-hat", sprintf("lat-hat-%s-%s-%s.rds", window_name, year_range, st_id))
        ## Default: no calculation failure
        lat_hat_error <- NA_character_

        ## Read existing result or calculate a new one

        if (file.exists(lat_hat_file)) {
            lat_hat <- readRDS(lat_hat_file)
        } else {
            lat_hat <- tryCatch(calculate_lat_hat(fit = fit), error = function(e) {
                    lat_hat_error <<- conditionMessage(e)
                    cat(sprintf(paste0("WARNING: LAT/HAT calculation failed for ", "%s | %s | %s\n", "Reason: %s\n"),
                            st_id, window_name, year_range, lat_hat_error))

                    tibble(constituent = c("LAT", "HAT"), value = c(NA_real_, NA_real_))
                }
            )
        }

        
        ## Check HAT/LAT values
        ##
        ## This is deliberately a very generous threshold. It is intended only
        ## to identify catastrophic numerical/extrapolation failures such as
        ## HAT/LAT values of hundreds or millions of metres.
        ##
        ## It should not affect plausible tidal estimates.

        MAX_ABS_TIDAL_LEVEL <- 20
        lat_value <- lat_hat |>
            filter(constituent == "LAT") |>
            pull(value)
        hat_value <- lat_hat |>
            filter(constituent == "HAT") |>
            pull(value)
        
        ## Determine whether the calculated values are numerically plausible
        invalid_lat_hat <- FALSE
        if (length(lat_value) != 1L || length(hat_value) != 1L) {
            invalid_lat_hat <- TRUE
            lat_hat_error <- paste0("LAT/HAT calculation returned an unexpected number of values.")

        } else if (!is.finite(lat_value) || !is.finite(hat_value)) {
            invalid_lat_hat <- TRUE
            lat_hat_error <- paste0("LAT/HAT calculation returned non-finite values.")

        } else if (abs(lat_value) > MAX_ABS_TIDAL_LEVEL || abs(hat_value) > MAX_ABS_TIDAL_LEVEL) {
            invalid_lat_hat <- TRUE
            lat_hat_error <- sprintf(paste0("Numerically implausible LAT/HAT values detected ", "(LAT = %.3f m, HAT = %.3f m)."),  lat_value, hat_value)

        } else if (lat_value >= hat_value) {
            invalid_lat_hat <- TRUE
            lat_hat_error <- sprintf(paste0("Invalid LAT/HAT ordering ", "(LAT = %.3f m, HAT = %.3f m)."), lat_value, hat_value)
        }

        ## If the LAT/HAT values are invalid, replace them with NA
        ## The tidal harmonic fit itself is retained. Only the unreliable
        ## astronomical extremes are removed.
        if (invalid_lat_hat) {
            cat(sprintf(paste0("WARNING: Rejecting LAT/HAT for ", "%s | %s | %s\n", "Reason: %s\n"),
                    st_id, window_name, year_range, lat_hat_error))
            lat_hat <- lat_hat |>
                mutate(value = NA_real_)

        } else {
            ## Save only valid LAT/HAT calculations
            if (!file.exists(lat_hat_file)) {
                saveRDS(lat_hat, lat_hat_file)
            }
        }
        
        ## Format output
        lat_hat |>
            select(constituent, value) |>
            mutate(window_size = window_name, year_range = year_range, lat_hat_error = lat_hat_error, .before = 1)
    })

## This is the sampling time, completed and standardised to 10 minutes
db_comp <- db |>
    select(-c(year, dtime)) |>
    mutate(time_rounded = floor_date(time, "10 min")) |>
    complete(time_rounded = seq(min(time_rounded), max(time_rounded), by = "10 min")) |>
